lead: A three-terminal IC regulator holds its output at a set voltage with almost no external parts. Inside one chip sit a voltage reference, an error amplifier and a pass transistor — the three blocks you built from discrete parts, now trimmed at the factory and guarded by current limit and thermal shutdown. A 7805 turns a rough 12 V adapter into a clean 5 V rail for a microcontroller; an LM317 sets any voltage a bench supply needs; an LDO keeps 3.3 V alive while a lithium cell falls to 3.6 V. Cheap, small, and on almost every board you will open.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.5 for the reference–error amplifier–pass transistor loop, negative feedback from Unit 4, and the thermal resistance idea behind heat sinks from Unit 3.

blocks.text: Chapter 1.5 built a regulator from a Zener reference, an error amplifier and a series pass transistor. The IC version puts all three on one die, adds a temperature-stable internal reference, current limiting and thermal shutdown, and brings out three pins: IN, OUT, and a common pin — GND on fixed types, ADJ on adjustable ones.

The loop is unchanged. An internal divider samples a fraction of Vout, the error amplifier compares it with the internal reference and drives the pass transistor's base. If Vout falls, base current rises, the transistor conducts harder, and Vout comes back. The divider ratio is trimmed on the die, so the part number fixes the output and no external resistor sets it. In symbols Vout = Vref × (1 + R2/R1), where Vref is the internal reference voltage, R1 is the internal resistor from OUT down to the tap, and R2 is the resistor from the tap to ground. For the LM317 the same formula holds with external resistors and Vref = 1.25 V, the OUT-to-ADJ voltage.

Two capacitors keep this loop stable. A 0.33 µF capacitor at the input stops oscillation when the regulator sits far from the rectifier and filter, because the wire between them adds inductance. A 0.1 µF capacitor at the output gives the loop a low-impedance path at high frequency and covers fast load steps. Some low-dropout types instead specify an equivalent series resistance (ESR) window for the output capacitor; outside that window they oscillate.

The 78xx family is fixed and positive. The last two digits give the output: 7805 is +5 V, 7809 is +9 V, 7812 is +12 V, and 7815, 7824 continue the pattern. A plain 78xx in a TO-220 package passes about 1 A; the middle letter gives the current, so 78L05 is 100 mA and 78M05 is 500 mA. Output tolerance is a few percent and dropout is about 2 V, meaning a 7805 needs at least 7 V at its input to hold 5 V.

The 79xx family is the negative twin: 7905 is −5 V, 7912 is −12 V. It regulates a negative rail and pairs with a 78xx to make the split supply a dual op-amp needs. Watch the pin order. In TO-220 a 78xx is IN–GND–OUT, while a 79xx is GND–IN–OUT. Swapping them destroys the part, and the pin order is a favourite exam question.

The LM317 is adjustable and positive, with pins IN, OUT and ADJ. Its only internal job is to hold exactly 1.25 V between OUT and ADJ; it has no connection to ground. Two external resistors turn that fixed 1.25 V into any output: R1 from OUT to ADJ (the upper resistor), R2 from ADJ to ground (the lower resistor).

blocks.where: Vout is the output in volts; R1 is in ohms from OUT to ADJ (upper); R2 is in ohms from ADJ to ground (lower); I_ADJ ≈ 50 µA is the current out of the ADJ pin, usually dropped because I_ADJ × R2 is only a few millivolts.

blocks.text: R1 is normally 240 Ω. It sets a minimum load current of 1.25/240 ≈ 5 mA, which the LM317 needs before it regulates cleanly; with no load the output can drift up. Output spans 1.25 V to 37 V, input may reach 40 V, and current reaches 1.5 A with a heatsink. The negative adjustable version is the LM337. Because the reference floats, the same chip also makes a current source: a resistor R from OUT to ADJ passes 1.25/R to the load.

Dropout voltage is the smallest input-to-output difference at which regulation still holds. Below it the pass device saturates and the output simply follows the input. A 78xx needs about 2 V; a low-dropout (LDO) regulator uses a PNP or PMOS pass device and needs 0.1 V to 0.5 V. That headroom decides whether a 3.3 V rail survives when a lithium cell sags to 3.5 V.

Quiescent current Iq is what the regulator draws at its ground or ADJ pin with no load: about 5 mA for a 78xx, a few hundred microamps or less for an LDO. It is wasted from the input and heats the chip.

blocks.where: Pd is the power turned into heat in watts; Vin and Vout are in volts; I_load and Iq are in amperes.

blocks.text: Heat leaves the junction through three thermal resistances in series: junction to case θjc, case to heatsink θcs (0.5 to 1.5 °C/W with thermal paste), and heatsink to ambient θsa. Add them.

blocks.where: Tj is junction temperature in °C; Ta is ambient in °C; Pd is in W; each θ is in °C/W.

blocks.text: Keep Tj below the datasheet limit, usually 125 °C or 150 °C. Efficiency is roughly Vout/Vin, so a 7805 running on 12 V turns 58% of the input power into heat. Above a few watts, use an SMPS instead.

figure.caption: The four regulator families and what each one holds. Notice that only the LM317 output is set by external resistors; the rest are fixed by the part number.

spec.aria: Tree of IC regulator families: 78xx fixed positive, 79xx fixed negative, LM317 adjustable and LDO low dropout.

examples.question: A 7805 has Vin = 12 V, Vout = 5 V and I_load = 500 mA. Its junction-to-case thermal resistance is 5 °C/W and case-to-heatsink is 1 °C/W. Ambient is 40 °C and the maximum junction temperature is 125 °C. Find the power dissipation and the largest heatsink thermal resistance allowed. Neglect quiescent current.
steps: Voltage across the pass transistor: Vin − Vout = 12 − 5 = 7 V.
Load current in amperes: 500 mA = 0.5 A.
Power dissipation: Pd = 7 V × 0.5 A = 3.5 W.
Check: 3.5 W × (5 + 1 + 18.29) °C/W = 85 °C, so Tj = 40 + 85 = 125 °C, exactly at the limit.
examples.answer: The 7805 dissipates 3.5 W and needs a heatsink of 18.29 °C/W or lower.
examples.check:
Vin = 12.0
Vout = 5.0
I = 0.5
Pd = (Vin - Vout) * I
Tj_max = 125.0
Ta = 40.0
theta_jc = 5.0
theta_cs = 1.0
theta_sa = (Tj_max - Ta) / Pd - theta_jc - theta_cs
print(round(Pd, 2))
print(round(theta_sa, 2))

traps: The LM317 holds 1.25 V between OUT and ADJ, not between OUT and ground. Grounding ADJ gives 1.25 V out, not 0 V.
The 79xx is negative, and in TO-220 its pins are GND–IN–OUT: pin 2 is the input, not the ground.
Dropout voltage and quiescent current are different things: dropout is the input headroom needed, Iq is the ground-pin current with no load.
In the heatsink calculation the thermal resistances add in series; forgetting θcs gives a heatsink that runs hotter than designed.
A 78L05 passes 100 mA, not 1 A. The middle letter sets the current rating.

quiz.q: What output does a 7905 give, and what is the pin order of a 79xx in TO-220?
quiz.a: −5 V; the pins are GND, IN, OUT.

quiz.q: Define quiescent current for a three-terminal regulator.
quiz.a: The current drawn at the ground or ADJ pin with no load; about 5 mA for a 78xx.

quiz.q: Why does the LM317 hold 1.25 V between OUT and ADJ rather than between OUT and ground?
quiz.a: Its internal reference floats on the ADJ pin. R1 from OUT to ADJ and R2 from ADJ to ground divide Vout down to that 1.25 V, so the output is set by the ratio and Vout = 1.25(1 + R2/R1).

quiz.q: Why is a 0.33 µF capacitor fitted at the input of a 78xx?
quiz.a: Long wires from the filter add inductance; the capacitor keeps the input impedance low at high frequency so the regulator's loop does not oscillate.

quiz.q: An LM317 has R1 = 240 Ω from OUT to ADJ and R2 = 720 Ω from ADJ to ground. Neglecting I_ADJ, find Vout.
A 7805 with 2 V dropout runs from a battery falling from 9 V to 6.5 V. At what battery voltage does regulation fail?
quiz.a: Regulation needs Vin ≥ Vout + dropout = 5 + 2 = 7 V. Below 7 V the output falls with the input, so it fails at 7 V.

quiz.q: Two designs give 3.3 V at 200 mA from a 5 V rail: a standard regulator with Iq = 5 mA, and an LDO with 0.2 V dropout and Iq = 0.5 mA. Compare their dissipation and say which advantage the LDO really offers.
quiz.a: Standard: (5 − 3.3)(0.2) + 5(0.005) = 0.34 + 0.025 = 0.365 W. LDO: (5 − 3.3)(0.2) + 5(0.0005) = 0.34 + 0.0025 = 0.3425 W. The dissipation is nearly the same; the LDO's real gain is headroom, not heat, when the input falls close to the output.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real LDO datasheets are dominated by stability: many ceramic-capacitor-stable parts give an ESR window, and some older PMOS types are unstable with very low-ESR ceramics. Modern designs push dropout below 100 mV using NMOS pass devices with a charge pump to drive the gate. Quiescent current in the microamp range decides standby life in a battery-powered meter. Search for LDO stability and ESR, or load transient response, to go further.
